sources.title: PSI record PSI-39: Cool Flames Investigation
sources.label: CFI
sources.text:
Investigation: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
Accession: PSI-39. DOI: 10.60555/m6pj-a914.
Project type: Microgravity Investigation. Flight program: International Space Station (ISS).
Dates: 10-01-2020 to 10-20-2021.
Hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
Objective: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
Hypothesis: Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
Approach: The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.
Research impacts: A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines. Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

sources.text: 1 Introduction Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and funda- mental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day which averages out to an astonishing 2.5 gallons per day per person (Reitz, 2013). The primary reasons for such a high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but globally, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability compared to many other forms of energy. With the emergence of newer internal combustion engine technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is more important that ever.
